name: Gagne
role: In charge of the Special Forces armory at the mountain; Larry says a French Foreign Legionnaire
summary: Named by Larry for the first time on 2026-09-01, in a telephone answer about why the radio site stood on the mountain. Describing an attack on the Special Forces camp at Đồng Xoài, he said the man on the other radio was "dying from shot in the stomach," and then: "Gagne was with me and died, he was a french foreign Legionair." Asked again on 2026-09-02 where Gagne was when he died, Larry answered: "No - he did not die. He was still alive when I got medivac out." Both accounts are his, given a day apart, and both are kept. The same day he placed Gagne concretely: he ran the Special Forces armory, and it was Gagne who signed out the Thompson submachine gun that stands against Larry's bunk in VN-0082 and handed it to him. His words are held in data/recollections/, where the fidelity travels with them.
researchNotes: The name and its spelling are Larry's own, given on the telephone and checked with him more than once; on 2026-09-02 his son also recorded the pronunciation as "Gone-yay". THE FATE IS CONTRADICTED BY LARRY HIMSELF AND IS NOT RECONCILED HERE. On 2026-09-01 he said Gagne died; on 2026-09-02, asked directly, he said Gagne did not die and was alive when Larry was medevaced out (data/recollections/giscus-stories-c18259589.json). Nothing is corrected in either record. The practical consequence is large: the earlier account made this a casualty search, and the later one makes casualty files the wrong universe of records entirely — a man who survived Larry's tour would not appear in DCAS or on the Virtual Wall at all, and searching there would return a meaningless zero. Nationality moved too, but only partly: asked whether Gagne was French himself he said "Yes, pretty sure," then immediately widened it — "He could have been born in Germany or Belgium, I don't know." That is consistent with the Legion, which recruits foreigners by design and has historically enlisted men under assumed identities, and it means a French national record set is a reasonable first place to look but not a safe assumption. Also recorded, and unresolved as written: "He did seem to care much for Lowry. Lowry was an alcoholic and Gagne didn't seem to drink much that I noticed." The first sentence reads as though a negation dropped out in typing, which would reverse its sense; it is quoted as given and not repaired, and the relationship between these two men matters because Larry believes Lowry is the likely source of the erroneous KIA report (see data/people/sgt-lowry.json).
